title: First yourself (157–160)
hookLine: set yourself in what is right first, then teach others; self is the lord of self

cards: You've met this person. The friend who gives brilliant relationship advice and hasn't had a calm week in years. The coach who yells about staying calm.

Maybe you've been this person, telling someone to get more sleep at one in the morning. Advice is cheap, and people can usually hear the difference between words that have been lived and words that haven't.
Chapter twelve of the Dhammapada is called self, and it opens with a simple order of operations.

teach.h: FIRST WHAT IS PROPER, THEN TEACH.
teach.b: Verse one fifty-eight, in Max Müller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer."
The old commentary pins this verse to a monk named Upananda, who gave eloquent talks about wanting little while quietly collecting robes for himself.

teach.h: ONE'S OWN SELF IS HARD TO SUBDUE.
teach.b: The next verse puts it plainly: "If a man make himself as he teaches others to be, then, being himself well subdued, he may subdue (others); one's own self is indeed difficult to subdue." Difficult.
The verse doesn't pretend otherwise. Then verse one sixty: "Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?"
In Pali it's short and rhythmic: attā hi attano nātho. A nātha is a protector, a refuge, someone you can lean on. But doesn't Buddhism teach anattā, not-self?

teach.h: A WEEK OF DOING IT YOURSELF.
teach.b: Here attā is the ordinary word for oneself, the way English says do it yourself. It's not a claim about a permanent soul. It's a claim about responsibility: no one else can train your mind for you.
That fits the whole week. No hiding place from your own deeds, papa. All tremble, so imagine yourself in their place.
The broken gong that doesn't answer back, kamsa. Fashion yourself, like water led in channels. The world burning, and the house-builder seen.

how: In Buddhist communities a teacher's own conduct is expected to match the teaching, and verse 160, attā hi attano nātho, is often quoted to mean that each person is responsible for their own practice.

o: put your own needs ahead of everyone else's
set yourself right before you teach others
trust only yourself, never a teacher

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: first what is proper, then teach

s: verse 160 contradicts the teaching of not-self
attā here is the everyday word for oneself, about responsibility, not a permanent soul.
verse 159 admits that training oneself is hard
"one's own self is indeed difficult to subdue."
the verse says never to teach anyone anything
it says first set yourself right, then teach.

games.q: you're Upananda. you've just given a moving talk on wanting little. back in your room, a pile of extra robes. what does verse 158 ask?
o: set yourself right first, then teach.
games.why: the commentary sets verse 158 beside Upananda's story: direct yourself first to what is proper, then teach others.

practice: Think of one piece of advice you often give other people: be patient, put the phone down, call your mother, drink more water.

Ask, gently and honestly, how you're doing with it yourself, not to scold, just to see, and if there's a gap, choose one small way to live it before you say it again. Then let the advice go quiet, and simply breathe.
